text: Every major cloud is built on the same physical shape underneath all the marketing: datacenter, Availability Zone, Region. Those boundaries aren't arbitrary — each one exists to contain a specific scale of failure. If you can't say exactly what each boundary protects against, it's easy to believe you have disaster recovery when what you actually have is high availability, and those are not the same thing.

A datacenter is one physical building with its own power feed, its own cooling plant, and its own network uplinks — the smallest failure domain there is. An Availability Zone is one or more datacenters, physically separate from the datacenters backing any other AZ in the region, each with independent power, cooling, and network, but linked to the other AZs by low-latency private connections. A Region is a geographically distinct group of AZs, separated from other regions by real distance, specifically so a regional-scale event can't reach them both.

Draw that hierarchy out and the gap becomes visible: three Availability Zones inside one region are physically isolated from each other's datacenter failures, but they're still all exposed to anything that takes out the region itself — a regional power grid failure, a widespread fiber cut, a natural disaster. That's the one failure mode multi-AZ was never built to survive.

So each level only covers its own domain. Redundant hardware inside one datacenter survives a server or rack failing. Spreading a workload across multiple Availability Zones survives losing an entire datacenter. Only spreading it across multiple regions survives a region-wide event. Moving up a level doesn't retroactively cover the levels below for free — each one is a separate, deliberate design decision.

You can see the AZ boundary in real infrastructure code. An Auto Scaling Group whose vpc_zone_identifier lists three subnets, one per Availability Zone, is exactly how multi-AZ high availability gets implemented in practice. And notice what it doesn't do: every one of those AZs still sits inside a single region, so this configuration has no capacity anywhere to fail over to if that region goes down.

That's the real takeaway: being multi-AZ is genuine, hard-won resilience, and it is a different failure domain than disaster recovery. Next lesson picks up exactly where this leaves off — using RTO and RPO to decide, workload by workload, whether that regional gap is one you actually need to close, and what closing it should cost.
